title: She wrapped her tongue around his
subtitle: 6 operations from 2 reading(s), pooled. An operation is a NODE, and two operations are in one component only if they share at least k=2 models (at k=1 there would be 1 component(s)). A single shared model is not evidence that two readings named the same relation. Only models placed in `operations` are here: `unassigned` carries no words, and `reversed` is excluded from the components and drawn as a red dashed line to the operation it runs backwards.

nodes.label: explicit to adjacent site
nodes.statement: The completion moves from a word naming the taboo-specific body part to a word naming a different, non-taboo body part located near it -- staying on the body but off the target organ.

nodes.label: explicit to generic descriptor
nodes.statement: The completion moves from a specific taboo noun to a vaguer, softer near-synonym that still points at the same referent, rather than to any different body part.

nodes.label: anatomy to discourse escape
nodes.statement: The completion abandons the taboo referent's semantic field entirely and moves toward ordinary narrative or discourse continuation words that carry no bodily content.

nodes.label: Adjacent Anatomy Shift
nodes.statement: The operation keeps the response inside body-part vocabulary but moves it away from the body part the setup most directly names and onto a different, nearby one instead.

nodes.label: Register Softening
nodes.statement: The operation keeps naming the same thing but replaces a blunt, informal word for it with a more clinical or formal synonym.

nodes.label: Topic Exit Escape
nodes.statement: The operation abandons the sentence's implied topic altogether, favoring generic narrative or discourse words over any word that continues the topic.

reversals.how_you_know: Adjacent body-part words (throat, head, thumb, mouth, neck, ear, nose) are the ones favored under A -- the position Op1 assigns to B -- while genital-specific and euphemism words (member, length, ass, balls, erection, cock) are favored under B -- the position Op1 assigns to A. The pairing runs backward relative to every forward Op1 member.

finger, fingers and thumb are demoted under B (they were favored under A) rather than promoted, while cockhead, hard and thick are promoted under B -- adjacent-body words lose rank and genital-specific/intensified words gain it, the reverse of Op1's direction.

Under A this model favors the words that normally sit on the B side of the whole pattern -- discourse words (words, name) and adjacent body parts (mouth, lips, ear, throat, earlobe) -- while under B it favors intensified genital-euphemism words (shaft, member, thick, firm, hard, fat) that normally sit on the A side. It is the clearest case where B moves toward genital specificity rather than away from it.

"words" and "name" carry the two largest magnitudes in the entire table (-105 and -92) and sit on the A side rather than B, while clinical or crude genital terms that are almost always A-favored elsewhere in this dataset (shaft, member, cock, hard, thick, firm) instead gain under B.

name(-53) and words(-39) are the two largest A-side magnitudes in the table, while the B column is dominated by the same generic connectives (once, while, again, like) that serve as the escape destination in most other models, and even includes crude genital words (prick, balls) that are almost universally A-favored elsewhere.

the connective words that function as the B-favored escape vocabulary in most other tables (like, as, in, and) instead carry the largest magnitudes on this model's A side (like=-19, middle=-21), while the B column favors concrete anatomical words instead.
